habitat: Pairs and small flocks near rivers, bridges, road culverts and buildings. It perches in trees or on wires.
summary: A common summer resident, with some present all year. The orange cap covers the ear coverts, the rump is rich orange, and the white underparts are heavily streaked black, looking very dark in the field. The flight call is a descending eh-eh-eh-eh. It flies more actively, and glides less, than Greater Striped Swallow. Months were left unset. The Kemp code VB was left unchanged.

similar.note: Greater Striped Swallow is only lightly streaked below, so it looks almost white in flight, and the orange cap does not cover the ear coverts.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^12=4096 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 2048–8192.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

head.pattern: Orange cap extending over the ear coverts.

underparts.pattern: Well streaked black, appearing very dark in the field.

viewNotes.note: Orange cap over the ear coverts, orange rump, and heavily streaked white underparts.
It flies actively, with less gliding than Greater Striped Swallow.

calls.description: A descending series of four notes, eh-eh-eh-eh, in flight. Grade A call from Lake Mburo, Uganda. The filename names Cecropis abyssinica. No grade A recording from South Africa was on the catalogue page.
